lead: Hydro sites differ in head and discharge. Three questions classify a turbine: does pressure fall inside the runner, which way does water move, and how much head is available. Engineers shortlist a runner type before calculation. Only a few universities teach this as a stand-alone topic.
prereq: You need velocity triangles and Euler's equation (6.2) and Bernoulli's equation from Unit 3, Fluid Dynamics and Flow Measurement.

sections.h3: Impulse against reaction: what the pressure does

blocks.text: An impulse turbine uses a nozzle to turn the whole head into a free jet at atmospheric pressure. The jet strikes buckets on a wheel spinning in air. Pressure at bucket inlet equals pressure at outlet, both atmospheric. Only jet speed and direction change, as in 6.1.

A reaction turbine has a flooded runner. Water enters at high pressure and pressure falls across the runner. Energy comes partly from falling pressure and partly from velocity change. The draft tube (6.6) lets a reaction runner sit above tailwater.
The separating number is degree of reaction:

blocks.where: p₁ and p₂ are static pressures at runner inlet and outlet (Pa); ρ is water density (1000 kg/m³); g = 9.81 m/s²; H is the head across the runner, total head at inlet minus total head at outlet at the same datum (m). R = 0 for an impulse runner. R > 0 for reaction, near 0.5 for a Francis and higher for a Kaplan.

blocks.text: High head gives a fast jet from a small nozzle; an open wheel is cheap. Low head needs large discharge, which only a flooded runner with large flow area can pass.
The second label is the water path inside the runner.

items: Tangential: jet along the rim in the wheel plane. Pelton.
Radial: enters at the outer edge, moves inward. Older designs.
Mixed: enters radially, leaves axially. Francis.
Axial: parallel to the shaft. Kaplan.

blocks.text: Pressure and flow direction are independent labels. Francis is reaction and mixed; Kaplan is reaction and axial. A closed casing does not make a machine impulse — only pressure drop across the runner decides.
Head is the third filter. Bands are rules of thumb; exact boundaries differ, but the order does not.
At fixed head, jet speed V = √(2gH), so one nozzle passes limited discharge. A multi-jet Pelton has two to six nozzles around one wheel. Jets raise discharge, not head.

figure.caption: First split on pressure. Inside each branch, head band and flow direction pick the family. Both reaction families run flooded, so only they need a draft tube.

spec.aria: Tree splitting hydraulic turbines into impulse (Pelton, high head) and reaction (Francis for medium head, Kaplan for low head) families.

examples.question: A canal site has H = 25 m, Q = 40 m³/s, overall efficiency 0.90. Choose a family and find shaft power in MW.
steps: H = 25 m is low head; Q = 40 m³/s is large discharge, so choose Kaplan (axial reaction). Pelton needs high head; Francis is medium head.
P = ρ g Q H η, with P shaft power in W.
examples.answer: Kaplan suits H = 25 m and Q = 40 m³/s. Shaft power at η = 0.90 is 8.829 MW, about 8.83 MW. Specific speed would confirm — see 6.7.
examples.check:
rho = 1000.0
g = 9.81
Q = 40.0
H = 25.0
eta = 0.90
P = rho * g * Q * H * eta
print(P)
print(P / 1e6)

traps: Calling Francis impulse because it has a casing. Casing proves nothing; pressure drop across runner decides.
Saying a reaction runner has no pressure change. Pressure falls across runner; that fall gives much energy.
Swapping labels: Francis is reaction/mixed, Kaplan reaction/axial. Neither is tangential.
Thinking more jets make Pelton reaction. Jets only raise discharge at same head.
Writing R = 1 for every reaction turbine. R = 0 for impulse; reaction lies between 0 and 1.

quiz.q: State the one test that decides whether a turbine is impulse or reaction.
quiz.a: Whether pressure falls across the runner: no fall means impulse; a fall means reaction.

quiz.q: Name the flow direction of the Pelton, Francis and Kaplan runners.
quiz.a: Pelton: tangential. Francis: mixed (radial in, axial out). Kaplan: axial.

quiz.q: Why is a Pelton wheel not sealed inside a water-filled casing?
quiz.a: The jet must stay a free jet in air at atmospheric pressure so its kinetic energy reaches the buckets. A flooded casing would submerge the wheel; surrounding water would slow and break up the jet, and efficiency would collapse. A Pelton has an open housing at atmospheric pressure, not a flooded casing.

quiz.q: A site gives H = 180 m and Q = 6 m³/s. Which family fits, and why?
quiz.a: H = 180 m is medium head, so a Francis (mixed-flow reaction) turbine fits. A Pelton needs much higher head; a Kaplan needs low head with large discharge.

quiz.q: H = 12 m, Q = 90 m³/s, overall efficiency 0.88. Find shaft power and name the family.
quiz.a: P = ρgQHη = 1000 × 9.81 × 90 × 12 × 0.88 = 9 323 424 W ≈ 9.32 MW. Low head with large discharge gives a Kaplan turbine.

quiz.q: Two sites each give 20 MW. Site A has H = 300 m, site B has H = 8 m. Explain why the runners look so different.
quiz.a: Discharge Q = P/(ρgHη), so Q at B is about 300/8 = 37.5 times Q at A. High head and small flow give a Pelton with fast jet and small buckets. Low head and huge flow give a Kaplan with broad blades and large flow area.

beyond: Not for exam. Pumped-storage Francis runners reverse as pumps; bulb and tubular turbines work at a few metres head; very high head sites use six-jet Peltons. Search bulb turbine, reversible pump-turbine and turbine selection chart.
